fact: Valrhona specialises in couvertures for chefs.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Valrhona's flavour wheel was created as a sales tool to sell couvertures for different recipes, rating intensity, roasted nuts, fruity, acidulous and bitterness from one to four pods.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Valrhona rates Manjari Madagascar 64% zero bitter, four fruity, four acidity, two nuts, one intensity, which gives chefs only basic information rather than actual flavours.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Mark describes Valrhona as a large-scale craft chocolate maker, and its Manjari 64% as a very popular chocolate.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Valrhona's Manjari 64% is acidic and chocolatey with lemon, raspberry and sour cherry; the group profile scored 86.03 from 678 tasters, though some batches can be woody.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Callebaut is one of the biggest industrial chocolate makers and processes roughly 39% of the world's cacao.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Callebaut's 'sensory language and tasting ritual' wheel tried to make commercial chocolate seem sophisticated, prioritising design over content, with odd neighbours like cashew beside caramel.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: A quarter of Callebaut's wheel is about mouthfeel, reflecting that the industry cares more about texture than flavour.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Cacaosuyo La Cuna 70% from Peru was sample one; the two-person group profile scored 91.9 (gold-level) with honey, raisin and dark sugar notes.
source: Webinar #2 - Introducing the IICCT profiling system and tasting practice
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Kuyay's Cuillay Yahuanga 70% from Peru (sample two) tasted fruitier and more tropical, with a quality score around 81 and slightly grainy melt.
source: Webinar #2 - Introducing the IICCT profiling system and tasting practice
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Two 70% Peruvian bars from different makers were chosen on purpose to show that cacao from different places and makers in one country can differ greatly.
source: Webinar #2 - Introducing the IICCT profiling system and tasting practice
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Kuyay's sample was mildly grainy, which a student linked to makers not over-refining to keep flavour; it was grainier than the Cacaosuyo bar.
source: Webinar #2 - Introducing the IICCT profiling system and tasting practice
speaker: student

fact: Lindt Excellence Origin Blend 70% (sample three) scored about 70 with high deviation and notes of coconut, baked chocolate and vanilla, below the 80-point fine-chocolate line.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Lindt's Excellence 70% tasted over-roasted, with ashy and burnt notes and an overall dirty, indistinct defect impression.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Lindt's cacao origin is not disclosed, but its coconut flavour suggests some West African (Ghana) commodity cacao.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Lindt's 70% bar has added vanilla (not from the cacao) that appears at the end and helps cover defects.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Lindt's sample showed a biscuit note, which Mark links to over-refining or over-conching friction; feedback to the maker would be to refine less.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Lindt's blended cacao appears to mix beans of different fermentation and roast, with rotting fruit, peaty and leather notes suggesting over-fermented lots and some mould.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Even the biggest firms like Lindt and Ritter Sport try hard to hide or cover defects with vanilla, sugar, heavy refining and smooth mouthfeel.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Ritter Sport Ghana 81% (sample four) scored about 60 with huge ashy and nut-skin defects, meaning over-roasting and high astringency.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Ritter Sport's 81% scored worse than Lindt's 70% partly because of the higher cacao percentage and the lack of vanilla to cover defects.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Ritter Sport's Ghana bar shows the coconut flavour typical of supermarket dark bars made from poor-genetics West African cacao.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Ritter Sport's 81% was rated clearly worse than Lindt's 70%, with fewer positive notes, more defects and a higher deviation.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm is a medium-scale craft chocolate maker from Denmark; its Nicaragua 68% (sample five) was a complex, defect-free bar with citrus, floral and a long aftertaste.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm adds a lot of extra cocoa butter, giving a mouthfeel close to industrial chocolate with a more complex flavour journey.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm's Nicaragua bar showed the creamy central chocolate note typical of Nicaraguan chocolates, plus citrus, tropical fruit, honey, rum and an olive-like positive umami.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Marou is a medium-scale craft maker producing big batches, offering traceability of its cacao and making an effort to source good-quality beans.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Marou's Vietnam 76% (sample six) was distinctive and polarising, with spices (allspice, black pepper), woody notes, dark fruit and dark sugars, scoring 81.68.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Mark does not think Marou's bar is over-roasted; its dark notes come from the nature of Vietnamese cacao, though it did show some real defects such as fermentation notes.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: A student sees Marou as a good entry point to craft chocolate because its dark, spicy flavours feel familiar compared with industrial bars like Lindt.
speaker: student

fact: Mark says Marou did not make its defects on purpose; the dark character is mainly the Vietnamese cacao, and there is room for improvement.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: Marou and Friis-Holm are both medium-scale craft makers, yet Friis-Holm gave a clean, bright, defect-free bar while Marou's was darker, spicier and polarising.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: A student who had liked Marou before found this sample raisiny, woody, earthy and astringent, unlike the bright citrus of the Friis-Holm bar.
speaker: student

fact: Mark calls the large amount of added cocoa butter a Friis-Holm recipe style that listeners can like or dislike but is not necessarily a defect.
speaker: Mark (teacher)

fact: A student who has tried many Vietnamese bars finds Marou's flavour profile polarising and says defects overwhelmed the positives.
speaker: student

fact: Ara Chocolat adds cocoa butter, partly to suit its French market and partly because its machines struggle with some cacao; it is also a deliberate stylistic choice.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Ara Chocolat's Las Violetas bar from El Salvador is 86% yet low in bitterness, showing that high-percentage chocolate can be pleasant.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Chocolate Tree's Arhuaco bar has added cocoa butter that Martin found slightly rancid, like old peanut butter, which dominated the top note.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Chocolate Tree is an Edinburgh, Scotland craft maker whose Colombian Arhuaco bar seemed to carry a fairly high level of cocoa butter.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Urá is a Peruvian maker in Lima whose Chuncho Señorita bar highlights the fruit of the cacao; Martin has known them five or six years and they have improved a lot.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Urá's Chuncho bar is two ingredients with no added cocoa butter, since these high-fat Peruvian cacaos do not need any.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Ura's Chuncho Señorita brings out much more fruit than Paititi's own Señorita, which tends to be woodier; Martin finds tasting them side by side instructive.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Martin contrasts Urá's fruity, lightly roasted bar with Morin's ashy over-roasted Chuao, calling it night and day.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Paititi's Señorita chocolate has a woody note and expresses less fruit than Urá's version of the same cacao.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona is a big couverture supplier by fine-chocolate standards but small by industry standards, with a few hundred employees and tens of thousands of tons a year; chefs treat it as a quality mark.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona dates from 1922 and took its name in about 1954; Robert Linxe persuaded the Bongrain dairy group to invest in it so it could make better chocolate for La Maison du Chocolat.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Robert Linxe founded La Maison du Chocolat in Paris after selling an earlier chocolatier chain, and it later spread to New York, Tokyo and airports.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona was a pioneer of acidity and fruitier flavour in French chocolate, a reaction against flat, low-acid, high-roast industrial chocolate, much like specialty coffee.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona launched its own couverture range in 1986 with Guanaja, Caraïbe and Manjari; Manjari was the first widely marketed country-origin chocolate since the 1920s.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona issued vintage bars with wine-style harvest years and specific places, publicised Chuao widely, and offered a Trinidad plantation bar and a Madagascar Criollo.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: In the last ~15 years Valrhona grew, lost the link between marketing and cacao, uses West African cacao under the same names, and adds much more cocoa butter, making it very soft.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona roasts in a medium-high French style but Martin has never had an over-roasted Valrhona, and nearly all its chocolates carry some acidity as a trademark.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona tried to compete more with Callebaut in recent years and moved away from its Criollo and origin story.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona Manjari gets its cacao from the Sambirano region of Madagascar, where Valrhona has invested; its problem is mediocre added cocoa butter and noticeable soy lecithin leaving an oily finish.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona also makes an 80% Madagascar 'confectioners' chocolate' with no added cocoa butter, which Martin finds quite good.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Martin uses Valrhona Manjari as a calibration chocolate when judging, but says its quality and consistency are not great; the current batch uses better cocoa butter than at any time in 10 years.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: The Valrhona Manjari sampled uses soy lecithin, which Martin tastes as a slimy, oily finish that makes the fat stick in the mouth.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Valrhona brought a range of flavours (fruity, citric, nutty, creamy) where Callebaut has no acidity or fruit; Martin says Callebaut is like an ashtray with bad cocoa butter masked by vanilla, and Valrhona is less bad.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Martin finds Callebaut chocolate completely lacking in acidity, with what little fruit there is coming from vanilla, and poor cocoa butter.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat dates from about 1880-1884 and, like Morin, survived without being bought out or merged; other European houses now belong to Mondelez, Nestlé or Mars.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat began its origin line in 1983 with Chuao, Ecuador and specific plantations, and was often first with a trend (Mexico, Piura, Chuncho).
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Stéphane Bonnat, the current generation, is planting Criollo clones in Mexico with his Mexican wife and local partners.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat makes about 600 tons a year of good-quality cacao, probably more than all European craft makers combined, yet is still family-owned and borderline craft.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat's roast has risen and become too high since the pandemic; Martin calls this its biggest problem.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat's 75% recipe is three ingredients (cacao, cocoa butter, sugar), implying 25% or more added cocoa butter, which tastes strongly coconutty and leaves a coating and plasticky feel.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat makes its own cocoa butter using Ivory Coast cacao, and said one of the year's two harvests is very coconutty.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bonnat has never used lecithin and adds cocoa butter for flow and tradition; a big part of its business is couverture and traditional French pralines.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Martin is a long-time Bonnat fan, calling it his second good chocolate; its Nicaragua, Brazil and Mexican bars used to work well with the recipe.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Felchlin of Switzerland makes couverture and some good chocolate (Original Beans, Chobba Chobba), about 1,700 tons a year, though not all of its cacao is great.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: After Valrhona, Felchlin (about 1,700 tons) is the next biggest producer with some fine chocolate, followed by Bonnat at about 600 tons.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Cluizel was probably the first to make high-percentage bars, with a 99% Noir Infini before Lindt launched its 100%.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: From around 2000 Cluizel launched origin chocolates such as Concepción (Venezuela, later lost to land seizures) and Los Ancones from Rizek in the Dominican Republic.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Cluizel long used vanilla subtly and well, but about three years ago removed it and raised the percentage of every bar, making the chocolate now poor according to Martin.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Martin says Bonnat still has good cacao with recipe problems that seem a choice, whereas Cluizel's chocolate has declined.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Pralus began in 1948 when the father's bakeries invented the praluline, a pink praline brioche; François Pralus later moved into chocolate.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: François Pralus owns a small farm in Nosy Be, Madagascar, and was early to explore odd origins such as Vanuatu, whose first chocolate tasted of bacon.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Pralus has about 60 stores in France and a few hundred tons of production, probably next after Bonnat, and is traditionally a high roaster, sometimes burnt.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Pralus's chocolate, even milk, was super burnt for 18 months about eight years ago because a roaster sensor gave the wrong temperature and nobody tasted it.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Bertil Akesson's London shop chocolate was mostly made by Pralus, with some by Bonnat and Morin, and was burnt too because of the same faulty roaster sensor.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Morin dates to about the 1880s, is four generations old, and made only couverture until about 20 years ago, when Franck Morin began making bars.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Franck Morin is open to exploring origins; some Peruvian bars like Chanchamayo are good, and he makes his own cocoa butter and cocoa powder.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Morin has raised its roast in the last year, perhaps to cover quality concerns; its Chuao tasted ashy and burnt.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Morin's Chanchamayo 63% was surprisingly its best bar a few years ago: very fruity, higher roast but not overwhelming.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: French roast style aims at chocolate, almond and lemon; Pralus was always prone to over-roast and now Bonnat and Morin are doing the same.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Martin links higher roasts at Bonnat and Morin to the cacao price bubble, with producers neglecting fermentation quality and makers roasting higher to hide defects.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Unlike Pralus, Valrhona, a much larger company, sits at the upper end of roast without ever being burnt.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Lindt launched the first 100% bar, after Cluizel's 99%.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Cocoa Town introduced the South Indian rice wet grinder, adapted for chocolate, into the US; these became the larger micro-batch refiners.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm is cited as a medium-scale maker working with half a ton to a ton of cacao, where a recipe error is a big correction.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Mars and Hershey began planting new cacao in Central America such as Soconusco in the early 20th century, reviving a region that had declined since the Spanish conquest.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Joseph Fry bought an English apothecary chain around 1750, an early example of chain stores and retail brands.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Most older European chocolate houses were absorbed into Mondelez, Nestlé or Mars, unlike Bonnat and Morin.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Pralus is a big French producer, probably next after Bonnat, not owned by a big commercial company.
speaker: Martin Christie (teacher)

fact: Duffy runs roasting tests (24, 26, 28, 30, 32 minutes), tastes each and picks his favourite, showing a two-minute change alters the profile.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Duffy's was the first UK bean-to-bar maker; he uses an old patisserie oven with a broken thermometer and roasts by feel rather than precise numbers.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Cacaosuyo supplied a Peruvian bar and a heat-damaged version for the defect tasting; the damaged one scored 72 against 86, losing bright red-fruit notes and tempering.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: A Domori Venezuelan 70% sample was found heat damaged and over-roasted, so it was flat, dry and crumbly; this may reflect shipping and storage.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Joy saw Cadbury's cacao in an Indian plantation left as a mouldy pile, because it is bought only to count as chocolate, not for flavour.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Cadbury's and Hershey's use so little cacao that its quality barely matters, thanks to milk powder.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Cadbury created the first box of chocolates in 1868, and its chocolate was known for being very sweet.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Fry's made what is thought to be the first commercial eating bar in 1847 in Bristol, the bitter, rough 'Chocolate Stick', followed by the mint fondant Chocolate Cream.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Fry's and Cadbury are the Quaker families of the UK; Cadbury's was very sweet while Fry's was bitter and called dark chocolate.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Casparus van Houten's cocoa press removed the fat to make cocoa powder, and his son alkalised the powder to reduce acidity and dissolve it better.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Henri Nestlé invented milk flour in 1867, and Daniel Peter then added it to chocolate to create milk chocolate.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Caffarel, Menier and Suchard in France, with Cadbury, Fry's and Van Houten, were 19th-century household-name chocolate companies.
speaker: Joy (teacher)

fact: Between the world wars Mars made heat-resistant ration bars for soldiers in North Africa, using lots of sugar and oat powder, deliberately without good flavour.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Godiva is a luxury brand that cuts cacao with cream, nuts and preservatives in pralines and fillings so the boxes last a year or more.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Godiva entered France in the 1970s backed by Callebaut, and this fuelled the 'finest Belgian chocolate' marketing campaign that persists today.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Cargill began planting cacao in Asia, mainly ICS-95, to reduce disease and war risk in Africa; this is why Vietnam, Papua New Guinea and Indonesia have good cacao.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: When the US candy industry took off, Hershey and Mars invested in growing cacao in Central America, mixing local criollos with imported trinitarios or amelonados, which displaced the old criollos.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm uses Ingemann's named Nicaraguan single varietals such as Chuno and Rugoso, which are planted, harvested, fermented and dried separately, and labels bars single variety.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: A set of Friis-Holm bars from different Nicaraguan varietals is ideal for tasting genetics side by side, since soil, climate, maker, process and recipe are identical.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ingemann's single varieties are used mainly by Friis-Holm but now also by many other craft makers.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Xoco Gourmet in Honduras grows the Mayan Red variety, used by a few craft makers.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Betulia, a farm in Colombia, grows three separate white-bean cacaos (B9, B6, B8) selected for flavour and kept apart from other cacao.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Rizek in the Dominican Republic plants and harvests local clonal varieties separately and grows neo-Nacionales descended from Ecuadorian Nacional.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Kokoa Kamili in Tanzania has had its cacao genetically tested and it is considered a neo-Nacional.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Domori uses Franceschi (Venezuela) cacao, but the teacher says its high roast partly destroys the cacao's character.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paradai in Thailand makes a Chanthaburi bar from selected white beans only, giving a very light brown colour.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Franco Cacao in Bahia, Brazil is a cacao genetics specialist as well as a maker, known for the cloned PS 1319 from Porto Seguro farm, a finalist in a local quality competition.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Franco Cacao uses careful fermentation protocols, drying and roasting to mitigate off-flavours in high-yield, resistant but weaker-flavoured varieties such as CCN-51, with limited success.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: In class tasting, Franco Cacao's CCN-51 scored far lower (66.8) than its PS 1319 clone (83.1), showing flat flavour, astringency, metallic notes and acetic fizz.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Tasting two Franco Cacao bars side by side contrasted the modern Trinitario hybrid PS 1319 with CCN-51, to teach recognising CCN-51 despite Ecuador or Nacional claims.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: The Jamaican 72% Bachelor's Hall Estate bar was rancid, which the teacher attributed to poor or old added decorative cocoa butter rather than the beans.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: The Jamaican maker uses very colourful packaging and splashes colour on plain bars, which looks like an inclusion bar.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Both the Jamaican maker and UK maker Pump Street make bars from Bachelor's Hall Estate; Pump Street's take is probably closer to European taste.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paititi, a family-owned farm in Cusco, makes a Chuncho mix bar using five-day fermentation, seven to eight days of drying and a gentle light roast.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paititi sometimes makes single-Chuncho-type bars but this one is a mix of different Chuncho subtypes grown in its area.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: El Rey is a very big name for craft chocolate in Venezuela and has used Ocumare 61, which has dairy, earthy, peach and floral notes.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ara Chocolat in Paris is one of the Venezuelan-run makers working with Venezuelan cacao despite export difficulties.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ara has made a limited bar with the rare Guasare white-bean Criollo, with a strong pistachio note.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ara's 70% Porcelana Criollo comes from the Caño de Tigre plantation in Sur del Lago (under a ton a year) and has no added cocoa butter.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ara's Venezuelan bar tasted creamy, smooth and European in style, scoring 91.55 in class, without any added cocoa butter.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Soma in Canada buys real Porcelana from a local genome garden rather than a farm, making its bar a good example of Porcelana.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Delirio is a women-owned Venezuelan maker based on Margarita Island that makes a 70% Choroni bar from Hacienda La Sabaneta cacao.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Hacienda La Sabaneta in Choroni, centuries old and once expropriated and abandoned, was revived in 2020 by the Gonzales family and grows old Criollo, Porcelana and local Trinitario inside a national park.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Valrhona pioneered origin couvertures and wine-style vocabulary such as Grand Cru in the 1980s, helping reintroduce origin to fine chocolate.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Valrhona's Guanaja, from Honduras, was its first origin bar and first Grand Cru, though it is probably no longer made.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Valrhona's early milk chocolate Jivara Lactée used smoky Papua New Guinea cacao and was popular, as smoke works in milk chocolate but is overpowering in dark.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Larger couverture manufacturers like Valrhona count as the regular fine-chocolate tier, above supermarket premium brands and compound chocolate.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Maison du Chocolat, with Valrhona, was an early bigger name that introduced origin couvertures to the market.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Valrhona, Cluizel, Bonnat, Morin and Pralus all adopted the wine vocabulary of origin and were true chocolatiers, making chocolate from the bean, selling to pastry chefs and retail.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Scharffen Berger started US garage-to-bar making and built its own machines for every chocolate-making step from scratch.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Unlike the big French makers, who kept old traditional grinders and big conches, early bean-to-bar makers such as Scharffen Berger built their own machines.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Amedei and Domori were the first in Italy to make chocolate from the bean on a smaller scale.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: El Rey in Venezuela was an important early participant in the bean-to-bar movement.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: The Grenada Chocolate Company, founded by Mott Green, was the first tree-to-bar maker; the term did not exist before it.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Pacari of Ecuador pioneered raw (unroasted) chocolate, is known for regional-ingredient inclusions and flavours, and still wins awards each year.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: These first US bean-to-bar makers shortened supply chains, bought nearly direct from farmers, and were transparent about cacao origin.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Early bean-to-bar purists made only two-ingredient 70% dark bars with no added cocoa butter to differentiate themselves from big industrial chocolate.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: CocoaTown, a US manufacturer, first imported Indian wet rice grinders for chocolate and recalibrated them for multi-day running; it now makes batches from 2-3 up to about 60 kg.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Duffy's in the UK was presumably the first micro-batch chocolate maker in Europe and still produces.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Fu Wan in Taiwan is a tree-to-bar maker doing high-end, nerdy fermentation experiments and nano lots.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: The Friis-Holm Chuno double-turned versus triple-turned bars were an experiment with Ingemann showing how one extra fermentation turn changes flavour, all else equal.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm follows the early French makers in adding a lot of cocoa butter to his chocolate.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm's main difficulty is finding stable-quality cocoa butter, which Lila thinks explains dustiness or off notes even though the beans and fermentation are fine.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: The cocoa butter in Friis-Holm's bars is probably not from Ingemann or the same variety, so any defect probably comes from it.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm wins awards most years with different products, showing persistent quality, though a given bar may not match the batch that won.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Students called Friis-Holm one of the greatest makers; the teacher noted he is not infallible and his bars can have defects.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Friis-Holm buys from Ingemann, a post-harvest processor and farmer, but not all cacao fermented and dried there is grown by Ingemann.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: The class describes Friis-Holm's approach with Ingemann as nerdy and tightly controlled, making mould in the fermentation unlikely.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Zorzal Reserve in the Dominican Republic grows cacao in its nature reserve and buys wet cacao from nearby farms, then ferments and dries it in its own facilities.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Kokoa Kamili in Tanzania is cited as a foreign-run central-fermentation model, not strictly a co-op, buying farmers' wet cacao.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Latitude Trade in Uganda is given as an example of a foreign company operating with cooperatives.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Zorzal and Kokoa Kamili are both similar to co-ops, central processors buying wet cacao, rather than classic farmer-owned co-ops.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paradai buys from two to three family farms in Chanthaburi and has won awards for direct trade; the International Chocolate Awards value traceability.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paradai's 70% Chanthaburi uses selected white-bean Chumpon 1 and 2 hybrids and a very low roast, giving an unusually light colour; other makers' Chanthaburi is darker.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paradai's Chanthaburi 70% has no added cocoa butter, only beans and sugar.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paradai's Chanthaburi cacao is intercropped with tropical fruits like durian and mangosteen, whose local yeasts probably add fruitiness to its fermentation.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Paradai is presented as a Thai tree-to-bar-style success showing Asian makers rising, and is the teacher's long-time favourite bar.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Norwegian maker Vigdis Rosenkilde makes her own batches of Peruvian-origin chocolate in the Cacaosuyo factory, selecting the cacao herself.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Cacaosuyo's factory in Peru hosts a guest maker, Vigdis Rosenkilde, who produces her own batches there.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Goodnow Farms made a 35-euro bar from the new white-bean cacao of a Matagalpa, Nicaragua farm (not Ingemann), with licorice and spicy notes.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: In Ghana all cacao is bought by the government body Cocobod, which regulates prices, so makers cannot pay direct premiums to farmers.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Unlike Ghana's Cocobod, Ivory Coast has no central government control of cacao purchasing.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Cacao Bisesto, a Matagalpa farm owned by Gif Laube, planted white cacao six or seven years ago and does fermentation and pre-drying experiments.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ingemann controls every fermentation step, including box temperature inside and outside and airflow, filling boxes with roughly 500 kg of beans.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Ingemann plants, harvests and processes each cacao variety separately on its Nicaraguan farms.
speaker: Lila (teacher)

fact: Baianí is a Brazilian brand founded in 2018 by a couple (Tuta and Juliana) with family roots in Bahia, often seen at international chocolate fairs.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Baianí runs many microlots to learn what genetics it has; its website describes a disease-resistant, productive hybrid of a Forest Area type and Trinitario, which Therese calls very generic.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Baianí makes the same bean in two roast profiles, called mild and bold, so tasters can compare how roast changes flavour.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: In Baianí's two roasts, the mild was sweeter with floral, honey and banana notes, while the bold gave more defined fruit (plum, raisin, prune) but lost sweetness and floral; Therese felt the bold was slightly ashy.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Duffy, a former Formula One mechanic, has 20-plus years in craft chocolate and works with an oven with stuck settings; he roast-tests by pulling a few beans every minute from about 15-20 minutes.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Fresco, near San Francisco, has long made a light, medium and high roast series and has stable settings, so batch-to-batch variance is low.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Fresco also offers a comparison range across conching time, giving a useful context, unlike makers who just say 'conched 96 hours'.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Fresco has won awards from the Academy of Chocolate, according to a student.
speaker: student

fact: Elemento, a Peruvian brand, has made a light, medium and dark roast series for five-six years or more; the roasts used to be more extreme and have grown closer.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: In Elemento's series, the light roast shows floral, honey and tight green-banana notes; higher roasts lose floral, gain sugar and bitterness, and give clearer fruit definition.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Solkiki is a very small, creative, vegan UK company using Peruvian Marañón beans (Fortunato No. 4).
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Solkiki normally roasts medium-plus but out of curiosity made an unroasted (raw) bar from the same beans.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Solkiki's unroasted bar is tight with grassy notes, green banana and honey, while the roasted version has more developed flavours but lost some lighter notes.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Therese uses Baianí, Fresco, Elemento and Solkiki as examples of makers whose roast comparisons show that lower roasts give floral/honey/tight fruit and higher roasts give defined fruit, darker sugars and bitterness.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Silva, a Belgium-based bean source, is praised for ethical sourcing and for publishing detailed write-ups of its trips to individual producers worldwide.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Manoa (American maker) and Dandelion made a series of interviews around cacao for Chocolate TV.
speaker: Therese (teacher)

fact: Goodnow Farms is named by a student alongside Fresco as an American craft maker.
speaker: student

fact: Bonnat was founded in 1861, remains family owned, and never sold out to an industrial producer; Stéphane Bonnat is the current master chocolatier making from the bean.
Bonnat tried origin chocolate in 1900 without success, revived it in 1983 with a full range (Ivory Coast, Madagascar, Chuao, Ecuador, Maragnan, Ceylon, Trinidad), and is still a leading origin maker.
Stéphane Bonnat makes award-winning chocolate and keeps exploring new origins and varieties, including a Soconusco bar named after Royal Cacao from Soconusco.
Valrhona, founded 1922 and renamed in 1947, launched its first origin 'Grand Cru', Guanaja, in 1986 with Robert Linxe; this helped start the fine chocolate revolution.
Valrhona's early Grand Crus: Guanaja (blend of 10 South American criollos), Carraibe (Caribbean blend) and Manjari (early Madagascan origin); first sold only as couverture to chefs.
Valrhona now processes around 10,000 tonnes of cacao a year, includes Ivory Coast and Ghana cacao, and Guanaja no longer mentions criollo or South America on its packs.
Valrhona introduced vintage bars with harvest year in the early 2000s, such as Gran Couva (Trinidad), Chuao (Venezuela) and Ampamakia (Madagascar criollo).
Valrhona's style is a medium-high French roast, good vanilla, soy lecithin, fine soft easily melting texture, and acidity as its signature note.
Valrhona was reinvigorated in the late 20th century by Robert Linxe, founder of La Maison du Chocolat, whose 1975 partnership led to the 1986 Guanaja launch.
Michel Cluizel was founded in 1947 in Normandy, offers origin bars and couvertures plus commercial lines like chocolate mushrooms and sardines, and is now run by Marc Cluizel.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Cluizel made high-percentage bars from 1990 (30g 'Noir Infini', only cacao and spices) and its first declared-origin bar, Concepcion (Venezuela), in 2000.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Cluizel's 'Los Ancones' single-estate bar uses cacao from Rizek's farms in the Dominican Republic; Rizek has one of the most advanced fermentation centres in the world.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Pralus is a family business that began with the Praluline brioche in 1948; François Pralus began chocolate making and owns a plantation in Nosy-be, Madagascar (2000), and works with 18+ origins.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Pralus's 'Pyramide' pack of 50g bars from different origins was an early way to sample origins and is still available.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: A. Morin (Donzères, since 1884, fourth generation Franck Morin) grows almonds, hazelnuts and sour cherries on the family farm and sources direct from plantations across about thirty origins.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Erithaj, Arnaud Stengel's brand showcasing Vietnamese cacao, is produced by Franck Morin combining A. Morin's expertise with Stengel's vision.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Ara in Paris is a new-style small French bean-to-bar maker that deviates from the highly refined, subtle palate of traditional French makers.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Hasnaâ Chocolats in Bordeaux used to buy couverture from large fine chocolate brands and now makes its own chocolate from scratch.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: Traditional French makers share a highly refined, subtle flavour palette; Ara (Paris) deviates from it with small-batch bean-to-bar work.
time: Producer styles — French fine chocolate makers

fact: After Valrhona's 1986 Guanaja, other established French makers (Cluizel, Bonnat, A. Morin, Pralus) took up origin chocolate and wine-style terms like Grand Cru, terroir and vintage.
Duffy's Chocolate (UK, Duffy Sheardown, Red Star Chocolate) pioneered use of Indian tabletop wet rice grinders for micro-batch chocolate, later adopted across Eastern Europe, Asia and Latin America.
Atlanta-based Cocoa Town imported Indian tabletop grinders that fuelled micro-batch chocolate growth in the USA and worldwide.
Scottish Macintyre and Barcelona's Lloveras are common machinery suppliers for smaller fine chocolate companies, often selling to upscaling micro-batch makers.
time: Producer styles — Medium sized/fine chocolate producers

fact: CPS Ltd (UK) supplies laboratory-sized bean breakers used by most small-scale makers and a winnower handling about 3-4 kg per hour.
The 'Crankenstein' is a hand-cranked bean breaker with a small hopper and toothed rollers used by small home batch makers.
Amedei and Domori (Italy), El Rey (Venezuela) and Scharffen Berger (USA) were inspired by the French new wave; Scharffen Berger founded the US bean-to-bar movement.
The Grenada Chocolate Company was the first 'tree to bar' producing company.
Pacari in Ecuador, producing in the country of origin, led the way in 'raw', minimally processed chocolate.
New US makers Amano, Askinosie, Patric, Rogue, Theo and Taza crafted chocolate 'true to bean', driving the US craft movement.
In the 1970s Belgian Godiva invaded France, creating a culture where 'Belgian is best' and texture was king.
Early chocolate companies Cadbury, Fry's, Caffarel, Menier, Suchard and Van Houten became household names and raced to make the first commercial eating bar.
Fry's of Bristol probably made the first chocolate bar, the 1847 'Fry's Chocolate Stick', bitter and rough with a fondant centre.
Casparus van Houten invented the cocoa press for extracting cocoa butter, and son Coenraad developed alkalising, making cocoa solids less bitter and more water-soluble.
Henri Nestlé invented milk flour in 1867, the first powdered milk, which Daniel Peter used to make milk chocolate.
Cadbury's introduced the first chocolate box of candies in 1868.
W. Jeffrey Hurst of the Hershey Foods Technical Center analysed Rio Azul Maya vessel scrapings and found theobromine, proving chocolate drinks about 500 AD.
speaker: Maricel Presilla (lecturer)

fact: Stéphane Bonnat used the name 'Royal Cacao from Soconusco' for his remarkable Soconusco bar, referring to the cacao the Spanish court kept with the royal jewels.
speaker: Maricel Presilla (lecturer)

Alex Rast, a Seventy% founding reviewer, helped IICCT evolve its flavour projection and profile system.
